This is the first movie I have ever had to turn off before finishing. I genuinely wanted to puke watching it. I am honestly baffled that this has been embraced as some kind of feminist fable. Strip away the elaborate production design, fish-eye lenses, absurd costumes, and self-consciously quirky performances, and what are we actually left with? A story about an adult woman whose mind is explicitly that of a young child being introduced to sex, prostitution, and relationships with adult men, and the film repeatedly frames this as liberation. Bella is learning to walk. She is learning language. She has essentially no understanding of social norms, relationships, sex, or the world around her. Yet we are expected to interpret her sexual curiosity as evidence of sexual empowerment. Her inability to comprehend what is happening is somehow transformed into an argument for her freedom. But a child’s willingness to participate in something does not make the adult exploiting that willingness any less reprehensible. “She likes it” is not the feminist defense this movie seems to think it is. And what exactly is the message here? That a woman discovers herself through sexual freedom and promiscuity with men? That apparently the great key to female self-actualization is discovering sex. It is an astonishingly narrow conception of female autonomy. The entire premise is disturbing enough, but the way the film celebrates it makes it substantially worse. Bella’s circumstances are horrifying, something that should invite discomfort is instead presented as triumphant self-discovery. The result isn't provocative feminism to me; it is a grotesque attempt to make exploitation look liberating by giving the exploited character a smile. And yes, the cinematography is impressive. The production design is incredible. The costumes are fantastic. The actors are clearly giving everything they have. None of that matters to me when the central premise is this repulsive. I genuinely cannot understand watching this and coming away thinking, “What an empowering story about a woman discovering herself.” What I saw was a deeply disturbing story about adults sexualizing someone with the mind of a child, then congratulating itself for calling that empowerment.

The art department absolutely ATE. Costumes, set design, make-up & sfx artists, visual direction…10/10 across the board, pure craftsmanship. As for the concept & screenplay? 2/10 A completely wasted opportunity. People keep calling this "subversive feminism," but the film’s actual structure tells a very different story. For over 80% of the runtime, we are forced to watch the voyeuristic objectification of a woman with the cognitive capacity of a child, left at the mercy of repulsive, predatory men. Calling this a 'journey toward sexual freedom' feels completely disingenuous when most of the movie is just a front-row seat to predatory men manipulating and mocking a woman's lack of boundaries. The supposed "subversion" is barely given any room to breathe. Bella’s actual intellectual, philosophical, and political awakening is crammed into the final act, acting as a thin, theoretical excuse to justify two hours of hyper-sexualization. There is a fine line between satirizing misogynistic reality and merely staging it for stylized entertainment, and the film crosses it completely. Stripped to its core, the movie spends nearly its entire duration packaging a deeply disturbing ethical conflict into a glossy visual spectacle. Wrapping predatory dynamic  in stunning aesthetics and calling it "liberation and empowerment " isn't subversive—it’s just intellectual laziness.

I really don’t know how to feel about this. The aesthetics are amazing and the idea is interesting, but there are things I just can’t ignore that make my experience watching this not as great as I would like. I can’t accept or pretend it’s normal for a grown man in his 30s to be lusting after and romantically captivated by a child in a woman’s body. To me, in all the sexual scenes, I couldn’t see anything more than men having sex with a child who doesn’t even understand what she’s doing and calls it “furious jumping.” She doesn’t have any actual idea about what’s happening and is driven by curiosity and the desire to satisfy the sexual urges that come with the body she’s now in. But that, to me, is still nothing more than a curious child trying to obtain “happiness,” as she calls it, through physical pleasure that she would otherwise have no understanding of if she hadn’t been placed in that woman’s adult body. Let’s not pretend that putting a feminist, female liberation framing around it makes something deeply disturbing any less disturbing than what it is: the sexualization of a character who is mentally a child, regardless of the fact that her body is that of an adult. All the amazing aesthetics and other praiseworthy visual aspects aside, this just ends up feeling like a poor representation of feminism through the eyes of a man. To me, if this was an attempt to make a statement and address the sexualization of children in today’s day and age, it failed miserably, because it ends up feeling more like a fantasy that normalizes the very things it tries to address.

Overall, I just didn’t get a sense of liberation from this. It felt more like a tragedy to me. I see that it is trying to critique the patriarchy and men who seek authority and control over women, but I didn’t necessarily feel that it fully succeeded at that either. I thought it was dark, disturbing, male-gazey, and that it didn’t necessarily know what it was trying to say. It was very artsy, the acting was phenomenal, and it was really interesting to watch, but I’m just not sure if it really succeeded in sending the message that it was trying to send. Poor Things é um filme fora do comum, que muito tem a dizer mesmo acabando extremamente limitado por um código fetichista que quase sempre desvia a trama do que realmente engrandece ela: o questionamento sobre a humanidade. A parte sexual, na minha opinião, é a parte mais controvérsa desse longa. É forçada, descaracterizada e de um mau tom terrível que pouco se justifica na trama. Deixando de lado a problemática quase capaz de desbloquear um novo terror feminino, a forma como o filme usa a sexualidade para interconectar a história é extremamente frágil e teria caído em total desuso se não fosse, ironicamente, a estranha e curiosa construção de mundo e desenvolvimento da personagem. Se tirasse a trama sexual, Bella Baxter ainda seria Bella Baxter, só que não haveria o teor extremamente doentio de sexualizar uma mulher com um cérebro de um recém nascido. A personagem atravessa um mundo exótico, místico, repleto de referenciais de baixa fantasia com folclore extremamente rico, rendendo até mesmo representações "a la inferno de dante" ao mesmo tempo que parece puxar ela constantemente para uma "comédia do abuso" que não agrega absolutamente nada a crítica e quebra a magia da experiência sem parar. O filme tem suas qualidades, mas sua estranheza sempre é sabotada, o que deixa extremamente raso nucleos como a questão do socialismo da personagem e sua evolução se empobrecerem para ceder a um clichê sem sentido onde em seus últimos 15-20 minutos ela decide trazer uma contextualização breve dos eventos que antecedem a história apenas para jogar no lixo toda a construção da personagem numa tentativa frustrada de um final anticlimatico e original. Então Bella fez o "pai" virar um bezerro (sendo cruel com o animal sem nenhuma razão ao retirar seu cérebro) e agora usa a segunda cobaia como serviçal? Qual o sentido? Ela não tinha acabado de dizer que não queria ser cruel? E além: por que ela acharia coerente informar o "pai" que queria ir embora após entender que ele era um maníaco armado? Para onde foi a evolução psicológica dela em Paris? O figurino de ponta e a atuação da Emma Stone podem ser um diferencial, mas essa história nunca deixou de ser uma colcha de retalhos.

Em vez de continuar desenvolvendo a mente e o intelecto em expansão de Bella, explorando sua forma única de descobrir o mundo, de construir afetos e de se relacionar com as pessoas, a direção prefere dar voltas no mesmo choque visual. Como dirigida por um homem, a experiência passa inevitavelmente pelo filtro do olhar masculino. *Poor Things* is one of the strangest stories of liberation I have seen because it asks a question deeper than whether Bella Baxter is free: who owns a person while they are still becoming? Bella begins as a creation. Godwin Baxter gives her life, names her, studies her, and keeps her inside a house where every part of her development can be controlled. The men around her initially treat her identity as something they can help design. Godwin sees an experiment and a daughter. Max sees a future wife. Duncan sees an innocent woman whose desire he believes he can awaken and possess. Each man loves a particular version of Bella, but becomes uncomfortable whenever she develops beyond that version. Bella’s existence is already a powerful metaphor. She has the body of Victoria Blessington but the brain of Victoria’s unborn daughter, meaning she is somehow both mother and child within the same body. She inherits a woman’s life without inheriting her memories, shame, or submission. Victoria ended her life to escape a world that controlled her. Bella is born from that ending and given the opportunity to confront the same world without accepting its rules. The film is often described through Bella’s sexual awakening, but sex is only the first stage of her freedom. Bella discovers pleasure before society can teach her to feel ashamed of it. Duncan mistakes this lack of shame for innocence and assumes he can turn it into dependence. Instead, every experience makes Bella more independent. He desires her most when she knows nothing, then begins hating her once she can question him. He does not love her freedom. He loves the fantasy of being the man who controls it. That is the pattern repeated throughout the film. Men celebrate Bella’s curiosity until it threatens their authority. Her innocence is attractive because innocence can be instructed, but intelligence is dangerous because intelligence can refuse. Duncan’s complete breakdown is hilarious, but it also reveals something pathetic about possession. He believes Bella’s desire belongs to him simply because he introduced her to a larger world. Once she realizes the world is larger than Duncan too, he becomes useless to her. Bella’s development is not only intellectual. It becomes moral. At first, she experiences life through appetite. She wants food, sex, movement, language, and anything else that produces sensation. The exaggerated colors and impossible cities reflect this stage of her mind. The world looks like a distorted storybook because Bella has not yet learned to separate beauty from reality. Her true awakening happens when she sees the poverty in Alexandria. Until then, freedom means doing whatever gives her pleasure. The suffering below forces her to understand that becoming human also means becoming responsible for other humans. Freedom without awareness is only appetite. Once Bella recognizes pain outside herself, her life gains an ethical dimension. She no longer wants merely to experience the world. She wants to understand why it is cruel and how it could be changed. Even her time in the brothel complicates the meaning of liberation. Bella believes she can separate her body from the shame society places upon it, but she also begins recognizing how economic systems turn bodies into objects. The film occasionally risks making sexual availability seem like the complete expression of freedom, but Bella eventually outgrows that limited idea. Her sexuality is one part of her identity, not its conclusion. She continues toward politics, medicine, friendship, work, and the desire to improve the lives of others. Godwin may be called “God,” but he is himself another creation. His father used science to mutilate him and called that suffering education. Godwin repeats part of that cycle by creating Bella as an experiment, yet he slowly learns to love what he made without completely controlling what she becomes. He gives Bella biological life, but he cannot give her an identity. The world gives her experience, and Bella finally gives herself meaning. This is why returning to General Blessington is so important. Alfie sees Bella only as Victoria, the wife who once belonged to him. He wants to restore the old order by controlling her movement, sexuality, and body. Bella is standing before the exact force that drove Victoria toward death. The difference is that Bella has developed the language, knowledge, and selfhood Victoria was denied. Victoria could only escape by destroying herself. Bella escapes by destroying his power over her. By the ending, Bella becomes a doctor and continues Godwin’s work, but she does not simply replace him. She becomes her own creator. The experiment begins studying the world that once studied her. The object becomes the observer. The body everyone attempted to possess becomes the home of a mind that answers only to itself. Yorgos Lanthimos makes every part of the film reflect Bella’s consciousness. The early black and white images feel confined and unfinished. As Bella experiences more of the world, color explodes across the screen. The distorted lenses make rooms bend around her, while the artificial sets remind us that society itself is also a strange construction. Customs surrounding sex, marriage, wealth, and gender only appear natural because people have repeated them for generations. Bella can see their absurdity because she enters the world before being trained to accept it. Emma Stone’s performance is incredible because Bella’s growth is visible in her body before it appears in her words. Her movements begin disconnected and impulsive, then gradually become controlled without losing their curiosity. Mark Ruffalo is hilarious as a man destroyed by the exact freedom he thought would entertain him, while Willem Dafoe makes Godwin both disturbing and strangely tender. The title *Poor Things* could describe nearly everyone. They are all creatures damaged by the people and systems that formed them. Godwin was shaped by his father’s cruelty. Duncan was shaped by entitlement. Victoria was trapped by marriage. Bella is the only one who examines what created her and consciously decides what she will carry forward. The deepest meaning of *Poor Things* is that being born is not the same as becoming a person. Birth gives us a body, but experience fills that body with desire, suffering, responsibility, and choice. Bella is created by a man, pursued by men, and repeatedly defined by men, yet the final person she becomes belongs to none of them. Godwin makes Bella alive. Bella makes herself human.

Eu acho que não estava preparada para o quanto eu ia gostar de Pobres Criaturas. Comecei o filme sem saber direito o que esperar e terminei pensando em como uma história tão estranha conseguiu falar de coisas tão reais. Com certeza virou um dos meus filmes favoritos. A Bella é uma personagem muito diferente. No começo, ela está literalmente descobrindo o mundo, mas quanto mais ela conhece, mais começa a questionar tudo ao seu redor. E é justamente aí que o filme fica muito interessante: Bella não aceita que outras pessoas decidam o que ela pode ou não fazer. Pra mim, uma das maiores críticas do filme é justamente sobre a liberdade das mulheres. Durante toda a história, homens tentam controlar Bella, dizer o que ela deve fazer, como deve se comportar e até o que ela deve sentir. Só que, conforme ela conhece o mundo, ela percebe que não precisa viver dentro dessas regras. Ela quer conhecer, experimentar, errar e escolher por si mesma. E gosto muito que o filme não transforme essa liberdade em algo perfeito ou bonito o tempo inteiro. Bella toma decisões que podem ser consideradas erradas, passa por situações desconfortáveis e descobre coisas difíceis, mas ainda assim são experiências que pertencem a ela. Pela primeira vez, ela está vivendo a própria vida, e não a vida que alguém escolheu por ela. A estética também é uma das coisas que mais me conquistaram. Tudo parece um sonho meio estranho: os cenários, as cores, as roupas e até os movimentos da câmera. É exagerado e bizarro, mas combina perfeitamente com a forma como Bella enxerga o mundo. E a Emma Stone está simplesmente perfeita. A atuação dela faz a evolução da Bella parecer muito natural, principalmente porque conseguimos perceber a personagem mudando aos poucos, sem ela perder aquela personalidade curiosa e completamente fora do padrão. No final, Pobres Criaturas acabou sendo um filme que eu não esperava amar tanto. É estranho, engraçado, desconfortável e bonito ao mesmo tempo, mas principalmente é uma história sobre uma mulher descobrindo que ela tem o direito de escolher o próprio caminho. Virou facilmente um dos meus filmes favoritos, e acho que é daqueles que ficam na cabeça muito depois dos créditos.

Poor Things es una película que entiende algo que casi nunca se muestra sin culpa: el placer de una mujer como motor de crecimiento, no como premio ni como castigo. Bella explora su cuerpo y el mundo con una libertad que incomoda porque no está filtrada por vergüenza, ni por la mirada de nadie más. Su deseo no es un conflicto, es una herramienta para aprender, decidir y moverse. Y verla disfrutar sin pedir permiso es, honestamente, una de las cosas más potentes de la película. Lo más interesante es cómo Bella se observa a sí misma casi como si fuera otra persona. No hay drama en ese desapego: solo claridad. Ella registra lo que hace, lo que siente y lo que cambia sin convertirlo en un discurso. Esa distancia le permite crecer sin cargar con expectativas ajenas. Es como ver a alguien construirse desde cero sin miedo a equivocarse. La película funciona porque no romantiza nada. No necesita metáforas para mostrar libertad, ni frases infladas para hablar de autonomía. Bella vive, prueba, se equivoca, disfruta y sigue. Y en ese proceso, la película deja claro que la independencia también puede nacer del placer, de la curiosidad y de la capacidad de mirarse sin juicio.

Poor Things: Slut-Shaming Happening Both Onscreen and Off When a film receives such high praise while simultaneously stirring up so much controversy, where exactly does the problem lie? Is it the film itself, the audience, or even society at large? The movie is saturated with explicit sex scenes—some have gone so far as to call it pornography, saying "male audiences are having the best time." Others have gone further, questioning whether the film is a faux-feminist work riddled with the male gaze (their reasoning being that both the screenwriter and director are men). Yes, the male gaze is indeed pervasive—but it comes from a portion of the audience's own male gaze, as well as from a strain of feminism so pedantic it engages in self-imposed moral policing. A feminism that stigmatizes sex and refuses to engage with it is, in truth, still thinking through a patriarchal lens. (1) Only "Sluts" Exist, Never "Man-Whores"? "The sexuality of a woman as private property is moral; the sexuality of a woman as a subject is immoral." This notion almost fundamentally encapsulates the logic behind most of the moral criticism surrounding this film. From a modern societal perspective, attaching moral constraints to sex is perfectly reasonable—the problem is that rather than applying such standards equally to everyone, patriarchy's stigmatization of sex is aimed specifically at women. So when audiences watch Bella on the big screen masturbating without an ounce of shame, having sex with various men, and actively choosing to become a prostitute, plenty of viewers conclude that Bella is a "slut." They see her becoming a sex worker as a form of self-objectification—even though Bella is far from ordinary, possessing none of society's ingrained moral constructs. She masturbates simply for pleasure; her sexual encounters with various men are entirely consensual—she is, as a subject, freely unleashing her desires. (Setting aside the question of whether unrestrained indulgence is justifiable, the key point here is subject versus object.) Yet audiences still insist on seeing her as an object, convinced that she has been reduced to a product whose purpose is to please men with sex. They believe that female sexual liberation is a form of self-deception, that in the end women are still being "taken advantage of" by men. So the film's abundant display of the female lead's sexual scenes actually carries no inherent sense of the gaze—it is simply presentation. Yet many female viewers feel uncomfortable with the sex scenes in the film, developing a sense that these scenes come from a male-gaze perspective. In reality, it's because they have preemptively placed themselves in the position of the object, the passive party—a mindset that presupposes oneself as the victim. So when they see the female lead's sex scenes, and it happens that the director is male, they begin to conspiracy-theorize that patriarchal forces are trying to reap benefits by encouraging female sexual liberation. They think the film is patriarchy's sugar-coated trap—but in truth, patriarchy's trap was already planted in their own minds long ago. It's worth noting that the rakish lawyer Duncan in the film proudly boasts about having slept with many women. No one morally condemns him for it. Offscreen, men are likewise never shamed for having extensive sexual experience—on the contrary, they're seen as "impressive." And yet this same Duncan still believes he has the right to criticize Bella as a slut. So it turns out only "sluts" exist—never "man-whores." (2) Enlightenment Through Prostitution? One of the film's most controversial plot points is Bella actively choosing to become a prostitute—and clearly maturing and growing through that experience. This has led many to crudely interpret it as the director suggesting that prostitution can foster a woman's intellectual growth. Admittedly, the film's chosen mode of expression is provocative, but this prostitution episode is more symbolic of what the world perceives as "depravity." "We must experience everything—not just the good, but depravity, fear, and sorrow too." This doesn't mean we all need to become sex workers; rather, it means that experiencing hardship does indeed open the door to a person's inner world of thought and spirit. Someone who has only ever experienced pleasant things is destined never to become a mature person capable of deep reflection. (3) Is the Film Advocating Sexual Liberation? What About Social Systems? So the film does explore desire, but its purpose is not to advocate unbridled indulgence. And desire comes in many forms—sex is merely one dimension of it. But undeniably, sex delivers the greatest visual impact, and shattering ingrained perceptions requires a certain degree of shock. Therefore, the film's abundance of sexual imagery is not trying to say that sexual liberation is the most important pillar of feminism, nor is it attempting to obscure other issues. It isn't even really a feminist film—one might sooner call it a libertarian film that takes a passing jab at patriarchy. Don't forget that Bella is an infant in a fully grown body, devoid of society's ingrained moral constructs, utterly loyal to her own instincts and desires. We can never become Bella. Rather, through the shock that Bella's behavior delivers to us, we become aware of how much society's concepts restrict our thinking—how they keep us trapped in perpetual cycles of self-moralizing and judging others. As a surreal film with absurdist themes, it is destined to be considered immoral by society's moral standards. Fixating on that point yields little of value. We don't need to—and cannot—become Bella, nor do we need to impose moral constraints on Bella or the film. But that doesn't stop me from intuitively finding something beautiful in Bella's purity. Ultimately, a film can never change society. When it tries to point out the absurdity of certain social rules, the public turns around and accuses it of being heretical. Perhaps it is destined to be something the masses cannot understand—poor things, pointing straight at you and me.
